content: Nuke the popcorn, fire up your TV, and get ready to laugh just for the fun of it with the perfect Labor Day film. We’re dusting off a comedy classic from the early aughts, and “White Chicks” makes one thing very clear: The joke’s on everyone. Black, Latino, Asian, white, skinny, fat, “differently abled,” man, woman, rich, broke, straight, gay — it’s all fair game. To add a little of Marlon Wayans’ main character energy as FBI agent Marcus Copeland, “Triple T-K-A … Time to kick *ss.” It took me a second to get into the flow of slapstick 2000s-era humor (did we used to have a longer attention span for gags that never end?). But after the first in a series of recurring jokes about Vanessa Carlton’s smash hit “A Thousand Miles,” I was sold and singing along. Makin’ my way downtown. Walkin’ fast, faces pass and I’m homebound . But I was in stitches when that milquetoast number set up a joke about a bunch of white girls (including Marlon and Shawn Wayans in whiteface) stuffed into a convertible somewhere in Long Island belting out the lyrics to 50 Cent’s “Realest N*gg*s.” Yeah. All the lyrics. The plot goes like this. Two disgraced FBI agents try to save their careers by signing on to the unenviable task of protecting two wealthy white girls from getting kidnapped in the Hamptons over Labor Day weekend. When the girls don’t want to go along with the plan, the Wayans brothers impersonate them. As they are forced to blend in with high society, shenanigans ensue. “White Chicks” feels like a guilty pleasure compared to more recent comedies that assign you the dubious homework of determining whether a blank stare and dry-as-dust one-liner count as “humor.” We accept this subpar invention as comedy, even though it has no effect on the corners of our mouths. Or souls. It’s intellectual, elevated, and award-winning. Hardy har har. “Mean Girls,” “Napoleon Dynamite,” and “Anchorman” also came out in 2004 on the coattails of blockbusters such as “Legally Blonde,” “Zoolander,” “School of Rock,” “Old School,” and “Dodgeball.” That decade, we also got “Superbad,” “Knocked Up,” “Forgetting Sarah Marshall,” and “Tropic Thunder.” All of these are worth watching again because they’re objectively hilarious. If not every joke stands the test of time, the freedom to laugh at anything reminds us that we used to have a collective sense of humor. Even the opening scene of “White Chicks” serves up the type of satisfying payoff great comedies once routinely pumped out for the popcorn-munching theater crowd. Instead of a climactic guilt-inducing lecture on how you could do better, there’s a choreographed impromptu dance-off. A “Carrie”-style paint spill to give the cartoon villains a taste of their own medicine. The brothers transform into white girls with mere seconds to spare, just like “Mrs. Doubtfire” did back in ’93. This kind of slapstick humor leaves no ridiculous stone unturned. But in the time since “White Chicks” came out, we’ve become dead serious ab
title: ‘White Chicks’ Proves Why A Lost Era Of Comedy Matters
author: Lauren Bair

content: Novo Nordisk has stopped two trials of a drug that aims to tame inflammation as a way to improve cardiovascular health, another blow for the approach. The company said it had halted the HERMES and ATHENA trials of its drug, ziltivekimab, after a data monitoring committee found they were unlikely to succeed. Novo informed trial investigators on Friday. The move follows the earlier failure of the drug in the ZEUS trial , which showed that the medicine, despite lowering markers of inflammation, did not reduce the risk of major clinical complications, including deaths and heart attacks. title: STAT+: Novo Nordisk stops two cardiovascular trials of drug aimed at lowering inflammation
